question: An 8-year old boy is brought into clinic for evaluation of possible scoliosis that was newly found on a routine exam at school. On exam, he is also noted to be in the 99th percentile for height and 70th percentile for weight. He appears to have abnormally long extremities as well as an upward lens dislocation on ophthalmologic exam. A mutation leading to a defect in which of the following proteins is the most likely cause of his condition?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Fibrillin -> Mutation in fibrillin gene -> Marfan syndrome presentation (long extremities, lens dislocation) -> 90% confidence. CHAIN: Fibrillin -> Defect in microfibrils formation -> Connective tissue weakness -> Marfan syndrome features -> 85% confidence. CHAIN: Fibrillin -> Abnormal fibrillin microfibrils in extracellular matrix -> Tissue laxity -> Marfan syndrome characteristics -> 90%
enhanced_information: The most likely cause of the boy's condition is a mutation in the fibrillin gene, leading to Marfan syndrome presentation. This is supported by the presence of long extremities, lens dislocation, and the role of fibrillin in microfibril formation. The evidence path showing the interaction of fibrillin with cells and genes involved in microfibrils further supports this conclusion.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case is the clinical presentation of a child with features suggestive of Marfan syndrome, including tall stature, lens dislocation, and long extremities. The mutation in the fibrillin gene is the most likely cause of this condition, as fibrillin is a key component of microfibrils and its defect is associated with Marfan syndrome.
